title: The time of Vespasian
hook: picture Vespasian's age: marrying, farming, flattering, all gone (Meditations 4.32)

segments.voice: Yesterday: do less. Your line was do less. Which task did you cross off, and did anything bad actually happen? Day five hundred fifty-nine.

Find an old photograph of your street, or your town's main square, from about a hundred years ago. Look at the people in it. A man in a hat hurrying somewhere. Two women talking outside a shop. A boy with a bicycle. Each of them was in the middle of something urgent: a debt, a crush, a quarrel with a brother. Every one of those urgencies is finished now. Marcus Aurelius did this exercise without photographs, using an emperor about a century before him. Today: the time of Vespasian.
screen: `A PHOTO OF YOUR STREET, 100 YEARS AGO.` → `EVERYONE IN IT, IN A HURRY.` → `THE TIME OF VESPASIAN.`

segments.voice: First, the picture. Think of the times of Vespasian, Marcus writes in the thirty-second entry of book four. Vespasian ruled Rome in the seventies of the first century, roughly a hundred years before Marcus wrote. Second, the list. And what do you see? People marrying, raising children, getting sick, dying, fighting wars, feasting, trading, farming, flattering, being stubbornly proud, suspecting, plotting, wishing others dead, grumbling at the present, loving, piling up treasure, longing for high office and for power. It's a list of everything people did then, and everything they do now. Third, all gone. And that whole life of theirs, Marcus says, no longer exists anywhere. Then he does it again, with the emperor Trajan's time, a little closer. Same list. Also gone. Fourth, why look. Marcus isn't doing this to feel gloomy or superior. He's doing it to measure. The quarrel that feels enormous this week is the same size as the quarrels in Vespasian's Rome. The flattering, the plotting, the grumbling: all of it went the way of the man in the hat. Marcus says to look at how many people threw themselves into these things, and then fell, and came apart. What lasts, for him, is not the outcome of the hurry. It's whether, in the middle of it, a person kept to what is right. The exercise shrinks the hurry and leaves the goodness the same size. That's the trade. Your worries get smaller. Your character doesn't.
screen: `THINK OF THE TIMES OF VESPASIAN.` · `MARRYING, FARMING, FLATTERING, PLOTTING.` · `THAT WHOLE LIFE IS GONE.` · `IT SHRINKS THE HURRY, NOT THE GOOD.` · then, large: `ALL GONE.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Picture the place you live, a century ago. The same ground, different buildings. People walking, working, worrying, each one sure their worry was the big one. Watch them for a few breaths. Then let the picture fade, the way it has. Now bring up one worry of your own and set it among them. Notice its size there. What's left that still matters? The bell holds the time.
The time of Vespasian. Marcus pictures Rome a century before him, marrying, farming, flattering, plotting, and notes that all of it is gone. Today's word.
Your line: all gone. When something feels urgent today, picture it in a hundred-year-old photograph, and see what size it becomes. Day five hundred fifty-nine.

howItsDone: Readers of Marcus Aurelius sometimes picture their own town a century ago, as in Meditations 4.32, to see their present worries at their true size.

fork.setup: you're losing sleep over who gets the corner office. what would Marcus's exercise in 4.32 do?
options: make the fight feel more important.
picture it in Vespasian's Rome, and let it shrink.
tell you to win at any cost.
fork.reveal: Marcus's list includes longing for office and power. all of it, he says, is gone. what remains is how you behaved.

original.note: Latin: the emperor Vespasian, who ruled 69–79 CE, about a century before Marcus.

trapdoor: what it means: picture an earlier age doing exactly what we do, and see your hurry at its real size.
what a scholar hears: Vespasian, Trajan, then Marcus's own court: the exercise walks forward through Roman history toward the reader.

notes: 4.32 paraphrased: consider the times of Vespasian: people marrying, bringing up children, sick, dying, warring, feasting, trafficking, cultivating the ground, flattering, obstinately arrogant, suspecting, plotting, wishing for some to die, grumbling about the present, loving, heaping up treasure, desiring consulship and kingly power; that life no longer exists; then the times of Trajan, all the same, also dead; consider how many after great efforts soon fell and were resolved into the elements. Confirm list and the 'fell and came apart' phrasing.
Vespasian reigned 69–79 CE; Trajan 98–117 CE. Confirm.
